```{r setup}
library(risikoR)
```

`risikoR` has four layers, each usable on its own:

* the **combat engine** — `rk_duel()`, `rk_duel_dist()`, `rk_duel_odds()`;
* the **battle simulator** — `rk_battle()`, `rk_battle_odds()`, `rk_odds_table()`;
* the **game model** — `rk_game()` plus the turn cycle and the AI agents;
* the **plot layer** — `rk_plot_map()` and friends, all returning ggplot objects.

## The dice duel

The heart of Risk is a dice duel. The attacker rolls up to three dice, the
defender up to two, and the highest dice are compared pairwise. The attacker
must roll *strictly* higher: ties go to the defender.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
rk_duel(3, 2)
```

`rk_duel_dist()` enumerates all `6^3 * 6^2 = 7776` equally likely combinations,
so the probabilities are exact rather than simulated:

```{r}
rk_duel_dist(3, 2)
```

`rk_duel_odds()` summarises the same enumeration:

```{r}
rk_duel_odds(3, 2)
```

The attacker expects to lose 0.92 armies and the defender 1.08 per three-on-two
duel — the standard textbook values.

```{r}
rk_plot_duel(3, 2)
```

## A full battle

`rk_battle()` keeps rolling until the attacker runs out of spare armies or the
defender is wiped out.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
battle <- rk_battle(10, 8)
battle
```

Every battle carries its own log, which `autoplot()` turns into a picture of
the fight:

```{r}
ggplot2::autoplot(battle)
```

## Conquest probability

`rk_battle_odds()` answers the question that actually matters at the table:
will this attack succeed? The `"exact"` method solves the underlying Markov
chain, so no simulation error is involved; `"mc"` simulates instead.

```{r}
rk_battle_odds(20, 15, method = "exact")

set.seed(1)
rk_battle_odds(20, 15, n = 1000)
```

Ten attackers beat five defenders about four times in five; the same ten
against fifteen almost never win:

```{r}
rk_odds_table(att_range = c(10, 20), def_range = c(5, 15))
```

## Setting up a game

`rk_game()` deals the 42 territories of the classic board and spreads each
player's starting armies over them.

```{r}
game <- rk_game(c("Red", "Blue", "Green"), seed = 1)
game
```

```{r}
summary(game)
```

```{r, fig.height = 5}
rk_plot_map(game)
```

## Taking a turn

A turn runs `reinforce` -> `attack` -> `fortify`, and every mutator returns a
new game object rather than changing the old one.

```{r}
placements <- rk_reinforcements(game, "Red")
names(placements) <- rk_territories(game, "Red")[[1]]
placements

game <- rk_reinforce(game, "Red", placements)
game$phase
```

```{r}
head(rk_legal_attacks(game, "Red"), 3)
```

```{r}
set.seed(42)
targets <- rk_legal_attacks(game, "Red")
game <- rk_attack(game, targets$from[[1]], targets$to[[1]])
game$last_battle
```

## Letting the machine play

`rk_ai()` builds a policy; `rk_play()` runs a whole game with one policy per
player.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
result <- rk_play(
  rk_game(c("Red", "Blue"), seed = 3),
  policies = c(Red = "aggressive", Blue = "cautious"),
  max_rounds = 30
)
result
tail(result$standings, 4)
```

`rk_tournament()` repeats that many times and reports the win rates, and
`rk_run_app()` opens the interactive Shiny application for playing, simulating
and analysing games.

Two further articles go deeper:
[playing a game](https://r-heller.github.io/risikoR/articles/playing.html) and
[the probability of Risk](https://r-heller.github.io/risikoR/articles/strategy.html).
